Quercus alba, Pinus echinata, Pinus rigida, Sassafras albidum, Oxydendron arboreum and Kalmia latifolia further away. Mature fruiting body (=FB) 4.0 cm tall. Immature FB 3.1 cm tall. Pileus dry; 2.2 cm wide in mature FB; 0.9 cm wide in immature FB; with whitish bloom toward center in immature FB; with small umbo in both FBs. Lamellae light yellowish-brown; sinuate; ~0.9 cm long at longest. ~36 full length lamellae present on mature FB (calculated by counting number in rough 1/4 and multiplying that number by 4). Lamellulae 3-tiered based on examination of photos. Stipe 0.4 cm wide at apex of mature FB; 0.3 cm wide at apex of immature FB; 0.7 cm wide at base of mature FB; 0.6 cm widest base of immature FB. Did not notice cortinas but there were small brown fibrils over the upper halves of the stems that were likely cortina remnants. Cheilocystidia absent. Basidia 4-sterigmate. This fungus was found growing next to an elm tree and marram grass in a moist environment. It was located about .5 miles away from the actual Lake Street Beach trail. It was also found growing in groups of twoâ€™s and threeâ€™s.
This fungus had a classic mushroom smell to it.
The pileus of this fungus ranged from 10 to 16 cm in diameter, and it had an orange brown color with concentric rings. Its surface was smooth, and its margin was smooth with a rolled margin. The overall pileus shape was infundibulum, and the inside of it was a creamy white color.
The gills of this fungus were adnate, and they had an even margin that was slightly eroded in some places. This was most likely due to the environment that it was found in. The gills were light tan in color, and they were approximately 1 mm wide. They were spaced about 1 mm apart. There were regular lamellae located near the edge of the pileus.
This fungus did not have a volva or an annulus.
This fungus had a stipe that was smooth, and it ranged from 3.5 to 4.5 cm in length. It had an overall tapered shape towards the base, and the inside of it was hollow. The inside color of the stipe was a creamy white, and it had a strigose base.
The spores of this fungus were light tan, and they had an ornamental shape. Their size ranged from 6.8 to 8.4 microns in diameter.
*Another key feature of this fungus was the white latex that oozed from the gills when they were cut or damaged.

Spores (mounted in diluted Congo red) 7.5-9.5 Ã— 7-9, with highly variable Q (globose, subglobose, broadly ellipsoid, a few verging on ellipsoid). Spores taken from both smash mount of gill material and two different prints. Spores obtained from smash showing globose nucleus (oil drop); spores from prints not showing oil drop.
Habitat for this collection is a small stand of mature Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) with a few small oaks mixed in. No hemlock in the immediate surroundings, but hemlock present in adjacent forest. I believe I have found the same taxon in another stand of Scots pine (not far from the location for this present observation), as well as in other areas with Norway spruce.
This type mushroom typically first appears during late spring in this same location (observed since 2011), as early as the first week of June. For this reason, I had originally considered Amanita praecox as its identity. But there are several reasons for my doubting these represent praecox: 1. Lack of hemlock in the habitat; 2. Range of spore quotient well exceeds praecox; 3. Occurrence includes springtime but this type also may persist throughout the summer into October (or may disappear in summer and reappear in fall). This year (2018) these did not appear in this location early August. (I checked often June-July.) First time seeing them this year (2018) was obs 327184.
But I still wonder if â€œpraecoxâ€ may apply to these. Another name that has been suggested is Amanita stranella.

MO Notes:
On lawn bordering woods with large shagbark hickory, large white pine, and several small oaks. The oaks are far enough away that I think itâ€™s unlikely any of them are associated with this mushroom.
Rain had just fallen, which is why the cap is wet and there are tiny beads of water on the stipe surface. Ground was very moist, apparently causing this mushroom to be fairly fragile. It broke apart as I attempted to extract it form the soil. Basal volva (detached) will be preserved and included with the rest of the dehydrated material.
Over the years, many similar mushrooms have been collected for this area (~30 square yard area part of which is sloped and part of which is level). A damp line of natural underground drainage runs through this area. The mushroom featured in this observation was collected from the level area. Specimens with the dark disc (like this one) as well as ones with more-or-less monocolor gray caps have often been collected from this same 30 sq yd area. Previously observed/posted (and also included in NAMP) is the observation obs 321879 , which features a monocolor cap, and which was found in the same 30 sq yd area as this present observation.
Found during same day in very similar habitat (but on other side of my house) is obs 328968.
The point here is to try to expand our understanding of the provisional species Amanita rooseveltensis. My understanding is that this species concept is based  upon collections of the monocolor types. Partly because both monocolor types and dark-disc ones are found in the same small area of my property, I think these may all represent the same taxon, A. rooseveltensis. My NAMP submissions of material representing both color schemes is meant to test this hypothesis.
The one seen in this observation has a particularly dark disc. Possible contributing factorsâ€¦ cap is unexpanded, weather is rainy. Or, the mushroom seen in this observation may represent a dark-disc rooseveltensis imitator (not actually rooseveltensis).
Both monocolor and dark-disc types collected on my property have consistently similar spore dimensions, mainly broadly ellipsoid 8-12 Ã— 7-9.

Stipe almost completely buried in mulch/soil. Hemlock dominated mixed woods with cherry, maple, and numerous beech trees of variable size.

Cap surface smooth with two thick patches of universal veil. Universal veil otherwise deposited along the stipe surface as fragile white plates. Deposits are seen clinging to the upper stipe near the cap margin, clinging to the edge of the partial veil, and lying near the specimen in the one photo. Presumably, some of the universal veil was lost in the soil.
Stipe with floccose scales/patches.
Some small areas of brown/gray stain developed, possibly due to the mushroom being handled. 20 hours after being collected the cap surface turned grayish with slight greenish tinge (7th photo).
KOH on cap surface negative (applied 20 hours after collection; bleached out the graying stain).
I think this mushroom represents a taxon that best fits into section Validae of genus Amanita. The provisional name Amanita maryaliceae has been suggested for similar collections I have made in the past. These may be viewed via the following links obs 171508, obs 210821.

Cheilocystidia is very heteromorphous, and I saw many forms and shapes that are not illustrated in the literature (see drawing). I looked at two individuals and they did not have pigmented cystidia, which all look consistently hyaline. This trait seems to vary according to a collection made around 2018 which I scoped with Jean Lodged and we found individuals with and without pigmented cystidia that otherwise agreed in all other traits observed. The publication â€˜New Species of Psilocybe in the Caribbeanâ€™ (2003) also mentions that a collection from the Dominican Republic â€œlacks the yellowish or grayish opaque pleurocystidia and the brownish or grayish opaque cheilocystidia that are typical of P. guilartensisâ€ but that â€œthe presence of the highly distinctive setaceous hyphae at the base of the stipe indicates this collection has strong phenotypic affinities with P. guilartensisâ€ and that â€œthe lack of pigmentsâ€¦might be due to the immaturity of the specimensâ€. This seems to be consistent with discussions Iâ€™ve had with Alan Rockefeller of the related taxa â€˜P. heimiiâ€™ and â€˜P. banderillensisâ€™ which may be conspecific but are designated based on presence or absence of pigmented cystidia.

I donâ€™t recognize this species, never saw it before at BBSF or anywhere else during my 10+ years of visiting the NJ Pine Barrens (I donâ€™t think this is A. longipes).  It appears to be a small-sized species, probably one of the smallest sect. Lepidella in my experience.  I found another collection of it down the road â€“ about 50-75 yards away â€“ consisting of several basidiomata, and the largest one at about the same stage of development was about the same size (see obs 466844).
The visible morphology is well documented in the attached photos.  The small size, the white woolly-felted to floccose volva breaking up into a dense network of patches on the cap surface and turning brown on the disk, the fibrous-floccose and rapidly evanescent partial veil and the densely woolly-floccose upper stipe (limbus internus?) are the salient features of this taxon. No odor was detected. 
 During the stipe expansion, the outer layer of tissue in the middle of the stipe cracked, giving the impression of a limbate volva.  The cross-sectional photo shows no saccate/limbate volva.
Overall fruitbody height = 7 cm; cap footprint = 4.5 cm; cap flesh = 8 mm thick above stipe; gills = 5.5 mm wide; stipe = 6.2 cm long, 1 cm wide at apex and gradually expanding to 1.2 cm just above the bulb; bulb = 2.7 cm long, 1.7 cm wide.  The spores appear high-end elongate to cylindric at x400 with no mounting agent; detailed measurements to be posted later.

A single fruitbody growing in shade on the side of a road cutting through a cedar swamp.  There were a couple of pitch pines (undoubtedly the host trees) nearby, but no oaks.
Overall fruitbody height ~ 6 cm.  Cap 7-7.5 cm wide (footprint), scarlet red with a mottled creamy-yellowish disk; cuticle dull, rough, somewhat finely granular, dry, not viscid, peeled ~1/3 at best; cap margin faintly striate and subtly tuberculate; cap flesh 7.5 mm thick above stipe. Gills 5.5 mm wide, appearing whitish to pale cream (spore print color probably B-D in Kibby Fatto), close but not crowded, not forking, with plentiful lamellulae of variable lengths.  Stipe 5 cm long and uniformly 2 cm wide, surface longitudinally textured and faintly flushed with pink here and there, not staining when handled. Cap and stipe flesh firm despite being a bit wormy, not staining when exposed to air.  Odor nill to faintly smokey(?).  Taste mild and pleasant (not chalky).
Based on the above characters interpreted with a bit of flexibility in stipe and spore print colors, this russula has the following codes in Kibby-Fatto book:
A = red cap
H = peels up to 1/3
K/L = stem white (K) or with just a flush of color (L)
N = cap 4-10 cm wide
P/Q = spore print pale cream to pale ochre
T = mild taste
Not surprisingly I couldnâ€™t key it out definitively.  In particular, the coniferous association was problematic.  The closest hits are R. cremeirosea and R. peckii.  Another possibility is R. subfloridana obtained from the southern species list.

The fresh tissue in buffer never got sequenced, but a dry voucher sample was eventually submitted to Steve Russell for ONT-nanopore sequencing.  The derived full-length sequence has a high RiC index of 243; itâ€™s uploaded to this post.
There are several accession of this species in GenBank, as demonstrated by their 99.2-99.8% similarity to this ITS sequence.  The species distribution range based on the accession metadata is southeastern Canada south to Tennessee and west to Michigan; some vouchers possibly came from Massachusetts and Ohio.  The Canadian accession, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nucleotide/OQ322226, calls this species Russula pulchra.  The other accessions are not named and Steveâ€™s â€œsp-IN110â€ is not there either (must be a code in his internal database).  The overall description of R. pulchra in Kibby/Fatto is in good agreement with the morphology of my specimen, including the odor and taste, but the habitat indicated in K/F (â€œdeciduous woods, especially under beechâ€) is very different from the Pinelands ecology my specimen came from.

The derived full-length nrITS sequence (ONT-nanopore) is 99.6-99.85% similar to 8 GenBank accessions, some of which are called H. subglabripes. Most of the associated vouchers originate from southeastern Canada (4), two are from Oregon (!), one is from NY state (my own obs 294169); the location of the last one is unknown.

As stated by me before, it appears that the distribution of H. subglabripes s. str. barely reaches the Mason-Dixon Line from the north.  However, itâ€™s possible that it can be found at higher elevations in southeastern Appalachia in mixed woods with hemlock and birch.  There is a lookalike species with a more southern distribution, exemplified by obs 244341 from North Carolina; its LSU sequence is only 97.2% (933/960) similar to that of MO294169 referenced above.  The three LSU GenBank accessions derived from Indiana collections by Michael Kuo are actually the lookalike of H. subglabripes.
